title: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde — Episode 3
subtitle: Robert Louis Stevenson's novella, continued: a friend who will not say his name, a face at a window, and a locked door that two men must break down.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this episode at A2/B1 level →  ·  ← Episode 2  ·  Episode 4 →
intention: you'll follow the story to the night the cabinet door comes down, and practise reported speech and orders — Poole said that he was afraid; Utterson asked whether…; the voice begged him to… — the grammar of a story that is pieced together from what people say.
previously: Two months after Jekyll's dinner, a maid saw Hyde beat an old gentleman to death in a moonlit lane: the victim was Sir Danvers Carew, and the broken stick was one Utterson had once given Jekyll. The police found Hyde's rooms in Soho, but Hyde had vanished. Jekyll, pale and shaken, swore he was done with him and showed Utterson a letter from Hyde. Then Utterson's clerk, Guest, laid it beside a note from Jekyll and saw that the two handwritings were almost the same, only sloped differently. Utterson locked the letter in his safe.
warmup: Last time you predicted what would happen next. Were you right?
Think of someone who suddenly stopped seeing their friends. What reasons can you imagine — and which one would worry you most?
You hear a voice through a locked door and it doesn't sound quite like the person you know. What would you do?
vocab_intro: Ten words you'll meet in this episode. Think first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: After the scandal the actor moved to a cottage on a remote island and lived in seclusion for ten years: no visitors, no telephone, no interviews.
items.meaning: seclusion (n) — the state of living away from other people, alone and hidden. Adjective: secluded (a secluded beach). A person who lives like this is a recluse.

items.sent: From the first scene of the film you know the expedition is doomed: the boat is too small, the winter is coming, and nobody has told the captain the truth.
items.meaning: doomed (adj) — certain to fail, die or end badly, whatever anyone does. a doomed love affair; doomed to failure.

items.sent: She had dreaded the phone call for weeks, and when it finally came she let it ring six times before she could make herself answer.
items.meaning: to dread (v) / dread (n) — to feel very anxious about something that is going to happen. I dread Mondays. She was filled with dread. Adjective: dreadful.

items.sent: The detective did not believe the old man had simply fallen down the stairs. The bruises on his wrists suggested foul play.
items.meaning: foul play (n) — a crime, especially violence or murder, as the cause of someone's death or disappearance. Mostly used by police and newspapers: Police do not suspect foul play.

vocab.heading: B · Which word means…?
vocab.instruction: Choose from: suspense · lurk · peril. Say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: …to wait somewhere out of sight, usually because you intend to do something bad?
items.meaning: to lurk (v) — A man was lurking in the shadows by the car park. Also used for bad feelings: a fear that lurks at the back of your mind.
peril (n) — The ship was in peril. at your peril = you will be responsible for the danger. Adjective: perilous.

items.sent: …the tense, anxious feeling of waiting for something to happen when you don't know what it will be?
items.meaning: suspense (n) — Don't keep me in suspense — did you get the job? A good thriller is full of suspense.

vocab.heading: C · Choose the meaning — a / b / c

items.sent:
The refugees lived in abject poverty, with no roof, no clean water and no hope of either.
  (a) extreme and hopeless   (b) sudden and short   (c) hidden and secret
items.meaning: (a) — abject (adj) — at the very worst level, without pride or hope. Collocations: abject poverty, abject terror, abject failure, an abject apology.

items.sent:
For years the village doctor could not name the malady that kept the young woman in bed; today it would take one blood test.
  (a) a painful memory   (b) an illness   (c) a family secret
items.meaning: (b) — a malady (n) — an illness or disease; an old-fashioned, literary word. Also figurative: the maladies of modern life.

items.sent:
My grandfather annotated every book he owned: the margins are full of his tiny pencilled comments, arguments and jokes.
  (a) sold after reading   (b) read aloud   (c) added notes to
items.meaning: (c) — to annotate (v) — to add notes or comments to a text. Noun: annotation. an annotated edition of Shakespeare.

vocab_use: Which of the ten words could describe a house, which a person, and which a feeling? Some fit more than one — argue it.
Using seclusion, dread and foul play, predict what might have happened to Dr Jekyll since the letter was locked in the safe.
story_intro: Stevenson's own text, shortened: the chapters “Incident of Dr Lanyon”, “Incident at the Window” and “The Last Night”. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

check.q: How did Jekyll's life change in the two months after Hyde disappeared — and what happened after the dinner on 8th January?
check.a: He came out of his seclusion, saw his friends again, did good works and was “at peace”. Then, from the 12th, the door was shut: Poole said the doctor was confined to the house and saw no one.

check.q: What does Lanyon say about Jekyll, and what does he tell Utterson to do?
check.a: He wants to see or hear no more of Jekyll and regards him as dead. If Utterson wants to know why, he must “ask himself” — and some day, after Lanyon is dead, he may learn the right and wrong of it.

check.q: What is written on the second envelope inside Lanyon's letter, and why does it shock Utterson?
check.a: “Not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll.” The word disappearance is the same strange idea as in Jekyll's will, which Utterson believed came from Hyde.

story.discuss: Utterson has every right to open the inner envelope — his friend is dead and nobody would ever know. He locks it in the safe instead. Is that loyalty, professional duty, or fear of what he'd find?

check.q: What do Utterson and Enfield see at the window, and how do they react?
check.a: Jekyll is sitting sadly by the half-open window, chatting; suddenly his smile is “struck out of his face” by abject terror and despair, and the window is thrust down. They leave in silence, pale, and Utterson says, “God forgive us.”

check.q: Why is Poole sure that the voice in the cabinet is not his master's?
check.a: He has been twenty years in the house and knows Jekyll's voice. He believes his master was “made away with” eight days ago, when they heard him cry out the name of God.

check.q: What has the person in the cabinet been asking for all week — and what did Poole see in the theatre?
check.a: A particular drug: order after order to the chemists, each sample sent back as “impure”. Poole saw a masked figure, smaller than his master, digging among the crates; it cried out “like a rat” and ran upstairs.

story.discuss: Poole says the thing in the mask was “more of a dwarf”, but the note is “unquestionably the doctor's hand”. Line up the evidence on both sides. At this point, what would you believe?

check.q: What do Utterson and Poole hear while they wait in the dark before breaking in?
check.a: Light, odd footsteps going up and down the cabinet floor — not Jekyll's heavy tread. Poole says he once heard it weeping, “like a woman or a lost soul”.

check.q: What do they find when the door falls in?
check.a: A quiet, ordinary room — fire, kettle, tea things — and on the floor the body of Edward Hyde, dressed in clothes far too large for him, with a crushed phial in his hand. Of Henry Jekyll there is no trace.

check.q: Whose name is in the new will, and what does Jekyll's note tell Utterson to do?
check.a: Utterson's own, in place of Hyde's. The note tells him to read first Lanyon's narrative, and then, if he wants to know more, Jekyll's own confession.

story.discuss: The clothes are “of the doctor's bigness”; Jekyll's handwriting is on the desk; Jekyll's favourite book is covered in blasphemies in his own hand. Put these clues together. What do you think the two documents are going to say?

grammar.h2: Grammar — reported speech & orders: Poole said that…, told him to…
grammar.intro: Almost nothing in this episode is seen directly. We learn about Jekyll from what Poole says, what Lanyon refuses to say, and what a voice says through a door. When you retell a story like this, you report what people said — and the verbs move one step back into the past.
notes:
1 · Statements: said / told someone + (that) + the tense moves back.
• “I am lost,” said the traveller. → The traveller said (that) he was lost.
• “The train has left.” → The guard told us (that) the train had left.
• “I will wait.” → She said she would wait.   • can → could   • was → had been
Words for time and place move too: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.
say has no person after it (said that…); tell always does (told her that…).

2 · Questions: asked + whether/if, or asked + question word — and NO question order.
• “Is the museum open?” → She asked whether the museum was open.
• “Where do you live?” → He asked me where I lived. (not “where did I live”)
No question mark, no do/does/did: a reported question is a statement.

3 · Orders, requests and warnings: verb + person + (not) to + verb.
• “Sit down!” → The captain told the sailors to sit down.
• “Please help me.” → The child asked us to help her.   • “Please, please stay!” → She begged him to stay.
• “Don't touch the wire.” → The electrician warned us not to touch the wire. (not “to not touch”, not “don't touch”)

grammar.outro: Reported speech is how a story gets told twice. Next episode, the whole mystery is told by two men who are no longer alive to be asked any questions.

paras: This is the episode where the mystery closes around one room. Stevenson has spent two episodes letting us see Hyde from outside — in a street, through a maid's window, in a fog. Now everything narrows to a red baize door at the top of a stair, and the question is no longer who is Hyde? but who is in there?

Notice who becomes brave. Utterson is a cautious lawyer who would rather lock a letter in a safe than ask a question. It is the butler, Poole, who has been counting the days, collecting the notes, listening at the door and running to every chemist in London. The servants huddled round the fire “like a flock of sheep” know more than the gentlemen. In a book about respectable men keeping silent, the man who finally says there's been foul play is the one with nothing to protect.

And notice how quiet the horror is. The room behind the broken door is not a torture chamber: there is a fire, a singing kettle, tea laid out, “the very sugar in the cup”. What is terrible is small — clothes that are too big, a mirror in a room where no mirror should be, a holy book full of blasphemies in a familiar hand. Stevenson never tells us the answer in this episode. He lets two frightened men stand in the evidence and refuse, for a few more pages, to understand it.
questions: Lanyon was a man of science. What kind of “shock” could kill a doctor in a fortnight? What does his illness suggest about what he saw?
Jekyll writes: “If I am the chief of sinners, I am the chief of sufferers also.” Can suffering cancel out wrongdoing? Should it change how we judge someone?

Utterson warns Poole to say nothing about the note so that they “may at least save his credit”. Even now, reputation comes first. Is that a Victorian problem — or do institutions still behave like this?

The last scene is set up like a locked-room mystery — but the reader has probably guessed the answer long before Utterson. Does a mystery lose its power when you already know the secret? What keeps you reading?

speak.useful: Report what people said: Lanyon said that he had had a shock… Poole told Utterson that… Utterson asked whether… the voice begged him to… Poole warned him not to…. For opinions: “What strikes me is…”, “In Utterson's defence…”, “The clue that gives it away is…”, “I'm not convinced that…”.

tasks.label: Task A · Poole gives his statement (4 minutes)
paras: The police have arrived at midnight. You are Poole, and you must tell the inspector everything since the door was first shut — but you tell it reported: what the doctor wrote, what the voice said, what Mr Utterson asked you, what you told him. The dinner in January → the door shut → Lanyon's death → the face at the window → the orders to the chemists → the masked figure → the evening at Mr Utterson's → the voice → the axe → what you found.

Use at least five reporting structures (said that, told him to, asked whether, warned me not to, begged him to) and at least five key words (seclusion, doomed, dread, abject, foul play, malady, lurk, peril, suspense, annotate).

tasks.label: Task B · Too late? (4 minutes)
paras: Utterson says, “We have come too late, whether to save or punish.” Was it his fault? He saw the handwriting, heard Lanyon, saw the face at the window — and waited. Take a side: Utterson failed his friend or Utterson did all a decent man could do. Give at least three reasons, and deal with the strongest point against you.
Then swap and argue the other side for one minute.

tasks.label: Task C · Predict (4 minutes)
paras: What happens next — and what would have to be true for it to happen? Utterson is walking home with two documents in his pocket: Lanyon's narrative and Jekyll's confession. Choose what you think they will reveal, tell it as a story, and explain what would have to be true for your version to work. Use reported speech where you can: Lanyon will say that he saw…
menu: Lanyon's narrative describes one night when Hyde came to his house — and what Lanyon saw that night is what killed him.
Jekyll is still alive somewhere, and the confession is a way of disappearing for ever.
Hyde murdered Jekyll long ago, and has been living as him ever since.
The drug Poole has been buying is the key to everything, and the “impure” samples explain why Jekyll could not come back.
The confession is not about crime at all, but about what every respectable person hides.
Utterson decides to burn both documents unread, and we never learn the truth from him.

final: Enfield and Utterson see Jekyll's face for one second and walk away without a word. Have you ever seen something you decided not to talk about? Why do people do that?
Poole knows his master by the sound of his feet and where his head comes to in the doorway. How well do you think we can really know the people we live or work with?
Lanyon says: “I sometimes think if we knew all, we should be more glad to get away.” What might a person learn that makes the world feel unbearable?

Before you go — from memory: report three things from this episode — one statement (Lanyon said that…), one question (Utterson asked whether…) and one order or warning (Poole warned him not to…). Then tell me what is wrong with: He asked Poole what was he afraid of.
